title: Mediated popular power
publishable_sentence: Representative democracy does not transmit a single unmediated “popular will” directly into government; individual political choices are filtered through franchise rules, representation, parties, electoral institutions and administrative procedures.
direct_primary_source: U.S./Canadian constitutional and electoral rules; source packet Window A/B.
best_secondary_source: Bernard Manin, *The Principles of Representative Government*; comparative electoral-system scholarship.
counterevidence_boundary: Mediation does not imply fraud or absence of genuine popular influence.
effect_denominator: N/A.
jurisdiction: General representative democracies; specific mechanisms differ by country.
cannot_claim: “Democracy is fake.”
chapter_destination: Foundation — What exactly are we calling democracy?

title: Franchise was constructed and repeatedly redesigned
publishable_sentence: In both the United States and Canada, the electorate was repeatedly expanded, contracted and institutionally redesigned rather than moving in a simple straight line toward universal participation.
direct_primary_source: Voting statutes, constitutional amendments, Canada Elections Act history; Window B source packet.
best_secondary_source: Alexander Keyssar; Elections Canada historical synthesis.
counterevidence_boundary: Long-run expansion of voting rights remains real despite reversals.
effect_denominator: Historical electorate sizes where used must include denominator.
cannot_claim: “More voters caused democratic decline.”

title: Majority procedure does not create unlimited jurisdiction
publishable_sentence: Majority rule is a decision procedure within a political jurisdiction; by itself it does not establish that every subject is legitimately open to majority control.
direct_primary_source: Locke, Madison, Tocqueville, Mill, Kant, Rawls and constitutional rights traditions.
counterevidence_boundary: The legitimate boundary of collective jurisdiction is deeply contested.
effect_denominator: N/A.
cannot_claim: “Any law supported by 51% is morally legitimate.”
chapter_destination: The Outvoted Person / Authority → Process → Scope → Liberty.

title: Large-scale politics generates specialization
publishable_sentence: Large representative systems generate specialized political intermediaries—parties, staff, bureaucracies, consultants, lobbyists and experts—because continuous political administration exceeds what ordinary citizens can perform directly.
direct_primary_source: Party/bureaucratic institutional records.
best_secondary_source: Michels, Schumpeter, Dahl, Weber, modern party-organization literature.
counterevidence_boundary: Specialization does not prove a closed oligarchy; elections, competing elites, insurgencies and reforms can disrupt insiders.
effect_denominator: N/A.
cannot_claim: “A closed political caste controls everything.”

title: Human motives are mixed
publishable_sentence: Human political and social behaviour cannot be reduced to material self-interest; reciprocity, fairness, identity, status, moral conviction, altruism and punishment of norm violators also shape behaviour.
direct_primary_source: Experimental public-goods, ultimatum and costly-punishment studies in source packet.
best_secondary_source: Behavioural economics / cooperation literature; Ostrom as institutional extension.
counterevidence_boundary: Self-interest remains important and often grows under anonymity, one-shot interaction or weak accountability.
effect_denominator: Roughly half conditional cooperators in some classic public-goods paradigms; exact numbers require direct-paper audit before publication.
jurisdiction: Cross-cultural behavioural research, not all political contexts equally.
cannot_claim: “Humans only seek advantage.”

title: Citizens necessarily rely on mediated representations
publishable_sentence: Citizens cannot directly observe most national political reality and therefore form judgments using mediated information, heuristics, institutions and trusted intermediaries.
direct_primary_source: Lippmann, *Public Opinion* / *The Phantom Public*; Dewey, *The Public and Its Problems*.
counterevidence_boundary: Reliance on cues can be rational and sometimes produces competent choices.
effect_denominator: Heuristic performance varies by sophistication and cue reliability.
cannot_claim: “Low-information voters are necessarily incompetent.”

title: Influence technology changed capabilities
publishable_sentence: From print through broadcast media, polling, voter databases and digital platforms, political communication acquired progressively greater reach, speed, measurement, segmentation and personalization.
direct_primary_source: archival media/campaign sources in Window H.
counterevidence_boundary: New capability does not prove large election effects.
effect_denominator: Tool-specific.
cannot_claim: “Each new medium decided elections.”

title: Polling made the electorate measurable
publishable_sentence: Scientific polling transformed public opinion from something political actors mainly inferred through anecdotes and organization into something they could repeatedly sample and quantify.
direct_primary_source: Gallup / 1936 polling records.
counterevidence_boundary: Sampling error, nonresponse and measurement choices can produce serious failures.
effect_denominator: Historical poll errors must be source-specific.
cannot_claim: “Polls reveal a pure popular will.”

title: Voter analytics separate prediction from persuasion
publishable_sentence: Modern campaigns can estimate turnout, support and persuasion probabilities and use them to allocate resources, but predictive classification should not be confused with demonstrated power to change a person’s vote.
direct_primary_source: modern campaign/voter-file methods.
counterevidence_boundary: Predictive scores can still matter operationally even when persuasion effects are small.
effect_denominator: Tool-specific; direct effect estimates require paper-level audit.
cannot_claim: “A campaign score means the campaign knows how to control the voter.”

title: Microtargeting is more clearly a delivery system than a mind-control system
publishable_sentence: Microtargeting can improve audience selection and message delivery, but evidence for large, precise changes in vote choice is much weaker than popular mythology suggests.
direct_primary_source: campaign experiments / Cambridge Analytica regulatory records.
counterevidence_boundary: Small effects can matter in close contests, and privacy/opacity concerns exist independently of persuasive magnitude.
effect_denominator: Precise ad-effect values remain on probation until direct-source extraction.
cannot_claim: “Microtargeting cannot matter” or “microtargeting mind-controls voters.”

title: Social proof is more reliable as a behavioural cue than a truth machine
publishable_sentence: Visible popularity signals can influence selection, engagement and perceived popularity, while their effects on whether people judge a claim to be true are mixed and often modest.
direct_primary_source: Muchnik et al. and social-proof experiments in Window K.
counterevidence_boundary: Topic, ambiguity, identity and platform format moderate effects.
effect_denominator: Individual studies report behaviour effects considerably larger than many credibility effects; do not generalize one study’s percentage across platforms.
cannot_claim: “Likes tell people what to believe.”

title: Missing denominator / exemplar distortion
publishable_sentence: Repeated exposure to vivid, unrepresentative examples can distort estimates of prevalence or social norms even when every example shown is authentic, particularly when base rates and selection mechanisms are hidden.
direct_primary_source: availability/base-rate/exemplar studies in Window K.
counterevidence_boundary: Some users infer selection bias, and explicit denominator corrections may have limited or heterogeneous effects.
effect_denominator: Project-specific effect size unknown until experiment.
jurisdiction: General cognition; digital-feed application not yet established.
cannot_claim: “Algorithms routinely make rare political behaviour look normal by a known amount.”

title: Reciprocal user-platform feedback
publishable_sentence: Users shape recommendation systems through clicks, follows, viewing and sharing, while those systems shape subsequent exposure; the relationship is reciprocal rather than purely platform-driven or purely user-driven.
direct_primary_source: randomized/quasi-experimental platform studies in Window L.
counterevidence_boundary: Relative causal weight differs by platform, design and outcome.
effect_denominator: Outcome-specific.
cannot_claim: “The algorithm alone radicalizes users” or “users alone create their feeds.”

title: Federal parties do not receive unrestricted access to the National Register
publishable_sentence: Elections Canada supplies eligible political actors with specified elector lists derived from the National Register; those lists contain limited fields and are subject to statutory use restrictions, rather than giving parties unrestricted access to the full Register.
direct_primary_source: Elections Canada / Canada Elections Act.
best_secondary_source: Office of the Privacy Commissioner guidance.
counterevidence_boundary: Parties can build richer records from other sources.
effect_denominator: N/A.
cannot_claim: “Federal parties get the full National Register.”
section: C. CANADA: POLITICAL DATA, BEHAVIOURAL SCIENCE AND COVID-19

title: Federal political-party privacy rules began with Bill C-76, then strengthened
publishable_sentence: Federal political-party privacy-policy requirements entered the Canada Elections Act through Bill C-76 in 2018 and were strengthened by later reforms, including Bill C-25 in 2026.
direct_primary_source: OPC 2019 guidance; Elections Canada 2026 C-25 guidance.
counterevidence_boundary: Exact commencement dates and specific obligations should be cited by provision.
effect_denominator: N/A.
cannot_claim: “Party privacy rules began with Bill C-47 in 2023.”
section: C. CANADA: POLITICAL DATA, BEHAVIOURAL SCIENCE AND COVID-19

title: Federal parties remain outside ordinary federal privacy-law coverage
publishable_sentence: Federal political parties are not generally governed by the federal Privacy Act or PIPEDA in the same way as government institutions or ordinary private-sector organizations, leaving a distinct election-law privacy regime.
direct_primary_source: Office of the Privacy Commissioner, 2026.
counterevidence_boundary: Election-law requirements have strengthened, and provincial law/history complicates the picture.
effect_denominator: N/A.
cannot_claim: “Federal parties are completely unregulated.”
section: C. CANADA: POLITICAL DATA, BEHAVIOURAL SCIENCE AND COVID-19

title: Bill C-25 added safeguards and individual breach notification
publishable_sentence: Bill C-25, enacted June 18, 2026, added new political-party privacy requirements including safeguards, notification to affected individuals in certain breach circumstances, and prohibitions on selling personal information or misleading people about collection purposes.
direct_primary_source: Elections Canada 2026; OPC Bill C-25 submissions.
counterevidence_boundary: The OPC still sought consent, collection/use limits, access/correction rights, regulator breach reporting and stronger independent oversight.
effect_denominator: N/A.
cannot_claim: “There is still no breach notification requirement at all.”
section: C. CANADA: POLITICAL DATA, BEHAVIOURAL SCIENCE AND COVID-19

title: Canada deliberately used behavioural science during COVID-19
publishable_sentence: Beginning in March 2020, the Government of Canada’s Impact and Innovation Unit and Public Health Agency of Canada ran an applied behavioural-science program explicitly intended to improve adherence to recommended pandemic behaviours; increasing COVID-19 vaccine uptake later became one of its stated objectives.
direct_primary_source: Impact Canada / PHAC, “Applying BeSci to the COVID-19 Response.”
best_secondary_source: Government publications implementing the WHO behavioural-insights survey tool.
counterevidence_boundary: “Behavioural science” is broader than “nudge theory,” and the existence of the program does not show every public-health policy was a nudge.
effect_denominator: Programmatic fact; not itself an effect-size claim.
cannot_claim: “The federal government secretly experimented on Canadians” or “every COVID measure was a nudge.”
chapter_destination: Government Learns to Measure / COVID case study.
section: C. CANADA: POLITICAL DATA, BEHAVIOURAL SCIENCE AND COVID-19

title: Federal vaccine messaging experiments tested behavioural frames and messengers
publishable_sentence: Federal behavioural-science studies tested how different vaccine messages and messengers affected Canadians’ stated intentions to receive a COVID-19 vaccine, including transparency, anticipated regret, personal/social benefits and source identity.
direct_primary_source: Impact Canada Vaccine Studies 2 and 3.
counterevidence_boundary: These studies largely measured **intentions**, not verified vaccination uptake; Study 3 found the tested frames performed similarly overall, with subgroup differences.
effect_denominator: Study 2 ~1,600 respondents; Study 3 ~2,300 respondents.
cannot_claim: “Those message experiments proved the government increased actual vaccination rates.”
section: C. CANADA: POLITICAL DATA, BEHAVIOURAL SCIENCE AND COVID-19

title: Behaviourally informed COVID communication was openly designed to motivate behaviour
publishable_sentence: Federal COVID communication guidance explicitly recommended behaviourally informed message framing—such as transparency, trusted messengers, efficacy/autonomy cues, moral values and pro-social norms—to motivate compliance with public-health guidance and vaccination.
direct_primary_source: Impact Canada, “Effective COVID-19 Communications.”
counterevidence_boundary: Recommended techniques were to be tested in context; behavioural framing is not automatically manipulation.
effect_denominator: Guidance, not a causal-effect estimate.
cannot_claim: “The existence of behavioural framing proves deception or coercion.”
chapter_destination: Persuasion, Manipulation and Coercion / COVID case.
section: C. CANADA: POLITICAL DATA, BEHAVIOURAL SCIENCE AND COVID-19

title: A nudge is not the same thing as a mandate or vaccine passport
publishable_sentence: Behaviourally informed communication and choice architecture should be analytically separated from vaccine mandates or passport requirements: the latter imposed material access consequences for remaining unvaccinated and therefore cannot simply be treated as ordinary low-cost nudges.
direct_primary_source: Canadian provincial vaccine-passport rules; project influence-definition framework.
counterevidence_boundary: Coercion exists on a spectrum; not every incentive or inconvenience is equivalent in severity.
effect_denominator: N/A.
cannot_claim: “All behavioural influence during COVID was coercion” or “passports were merely nudges.”
section: C. CANADA: POLITICAL DATA, BEHAVIOURAL SCIENCE AND COVID-19

title: Vaccine passports were associated with increased first-dose uptake
publishable_sentence: Quasi-experimental studies found that announcements of COVID-19 vaccine-passport or mandate policies were followed by measurable increases in first-dose vaccination in several Canadian provinces, although estimated effects varied substantially across designs and provinces.
counterevidence_boundary: These are quasi-experimental, not randomized; policies coincided with changing case rates, public concern and other interventions. In Ontario/Quebec, one study estimated only about 0.7–0.9 percentage-point additional first-dose coverage over 11 weeks from the passport announcement despite substantial relative increases in remaining first doses.
effect_denominator: Ontario + Quebec population ≥12: ~20.5 million in one study; estimated +0.7 pp Ontario and +0.9 pp Quebec. Other province-level analyses found larger estimated coverage changes in some provinces.
cannot_claim: “Nudge messaging caused these passport effects” or “passports alone explain national uptake.”
section: C. CANADA: POLITICAL DATA, BEHAVIOURAL SCIENCE AND COVID-19

title: A targeted Ontario practice-facilitation intervention produced a null uptake result
publishable_sentence: In a later Ontario cluster-randomized trial, offering practice-facilitation support to family physicians with many unvaccinated patients did not increase COVID-19 vaccination uptake in the intention-to-treat analysis.
counterevidence_boundary: Only 29% of intervention physicians accepted assistance; baseline vaccination was already high, reducing room for improvement.
effect_denominator: 582 physicians analyzed; adjusted RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.96–1.02.
cannot_claim: “Behavioural interventions never work” or “physician outreach cannot work.”
section: C. CANADA: POLITICAL DATA, BEHAVIOURAL SCIENCE AND COVID-19

title: Competitive adaptation does not require a mastermind
publishable_sentence: Under some incentive structures, campaigns, media organizations, platforms and users can adapt toward attention-maximizing or divisive tactics without any single actor designing the system as a whole.
direct_primary_source: actor-specific studies in Incentive Machine packet.
best_secondary_source: public choice, media economics, attention-economy and platform research.
counterevidence_boundary: Some institutions reward reputation, accuracy, restraint and cooperation.
effect_denominator: Mechanism-specific.
cannot_claim: “The system necessarily optimizes for polarization.”

title: Trump is a stress test, not the origin
publishable_sentence: Many features of contemporary U.S. polarization and institutional distrust predate Donald Trump, while his political style, celebrity, direct communication and conflict-driven media presence interacted powerfully with the mature social-media environment.
direct_primary_source: pre-2015 polling/media archives + Trump communication record.
counterevidence_boundary: Trump’s own actions and rhetoric can independently cause reactions; “pre-existing” does not mean “unchanged by Trump.”
effect_denominator: Trend-specific.
cannot_claim: “Trump caused polarization” or “Trump had no causal role.”

title: Canada is a rational-threat and source-cue comparison case
publishable_sentence: Canadian reactions to U.S. political leaders can reflect both real external consequences—trade, security, sovereignty and alliance policy—and source or identity cues; those channels must be separated rather than labeling strong Canadian reactions irrational by default.
direct_primary_source: Canadian policy events/polling.
counterevidence_boundary: Stable policy preferences can overwhelm source labels.
effect_denominator: Policy-specific.
cannot_claim: “Anti-Trump Canadian opinion is TDS.”

title: Source contamination remains testable, not established for Canada generally
publishable_sentence: Whether a leader’s name independently changes Canadian evaluation of an otherwise identical policy is an empirical question that can be isolated with randomized source-label experiments.
direct_primary_source: None yet for project-specific effect.
counterevidence_boundary: No meaningful label effect is possible if prior policy views dominate.
effect_denominator: To be preregistered.
cannot_claim: “A non-significant p-value falsifies contamination.”

title: Missing Denominator project effect is not yet an original result
publishable_sentence: Existing literature supports the mechanism strongly enough to justify a preregistered experiment, but this project has not yet shown that an authentic-but-selected political feed produces a practically meaningful prevalence error.
direct_primary_source: Window K background literature.
effect_denominator: Unknown.
cannot_claim: “Worst Five Minutes has been experimentally established by this project.”

title: Current empirical status
publishable_sentence: The project presently offers a strong synthesis of existing evidence and several falsifiable mechanisms, but no original causal result from its proposed human experiments.
direct_primary_source: Project evidence register / Window P.
counterevidence_boundary: Changes only after successful preregistered study + replication.
cannot_claim: “We discovered a new causal mechanism.”

title: Algorithmic exposure
publishable_sentence: Feed-ranking systems can materially alter the ideological, source and emotional composition of political information users encounter.
direct_primary_source: Nyhan et al. 2023; Gauthier et al. 2026; Brady et al. 2026; Ibrahim et al. 2026.
counterevidence_boundary: Exposure changes do not automatically produce attitude changes.
effect_denominator: Facebook n=23,377; X post-treatment n=4,965; Bluesky n=2,000; TikTok 323 successful audits and >280,000 recommendations.
cannot_claim: “Exposure change automatically causes opinion change.”
section: F. ALGORITHM OUTCOME AUDIT — DIRECT PAPER ADDITIONS

title: Algorithmic attitude effects
publishable_sentence: Randomized evidence from X shows that algorithmic feed exposure can shift selected issue and current-event attitudes over several weeks without detectably shifting partisan identity or affective polarization.
direct_primary_source: Gauthier et al., Nature 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10098-2.
counterevidence_boundary: Large Meta interventions produced attitudinal nulls; effects are platform/outcome-specific.
effect_denominator: X algorithm-on effects included approximately +0.11 SD conservative policy priorities, +0.08 SD Trump-investigation judgments, +0.12 SD pro-Kremlin attitudes, +0.12 SD combined political/current-news index; n=4,965 post-treatment.
jurisdiction: X users in the United States, 2023.
cannot_claim: “All algorithms push users in the same ideological direction” or “X converted users into Republicans.”
section: F. ALGORITHM OUTCOME AUDIT — DIRECT PAPER ADDITIONS

title: Social-norm distortion
publishable_sentence: Randomized feed-ranking experiments show that engagement-based ranking can distort perceptions of political social norms and increase perceived partisan animosity.
counterevidence_boundary: Perceived animosity is not identical to users becoming more hostile themselves; own engagement behaviour did not significantly change.
effect_denominator: n=2,000, 8 weeks around the 2024 U.S. election.
cannot_claim: “The feed made participants personally more hateful.”
chapter_destination: Crowd at the Cliff / The Crowd You Think Exists.
section: F. ALGORITHM OUTCOME AUDIT — DIRECT PAPER ADDITIONS

title: User-selection counterweight
publishable_sentence: User choice can make political information consumption more partisan than algorithmic exposure alone.
direct_primary_source: Robertson et al., Nature 2023, DOI 10.1038/s41586-023-06078-5; Nyhan et al., Nature 2023.
counterevidence_boundary: Strong platform ranking effects on exposure remain demonstrable; user agency does not make algorithms irrelevant.
effect_denominator: Study-specific.
jurisdiction: Google Search / Facebook U.S. election contexts.
cannot_claim: “Users fully control their information environments.”
section: F. ALGORITHM OUTCOME AUDIT — DIRECT PAPER ADDITIONS

title: Deep-attitude resistance
publishable_sentence: Large platform experiments frequently find that substantial changes in political exposure do not produce measurable changes in affective polarization or partisan identity over the study windows examined.
direct_primary_source: Nyhan et al. 2023; Gauthier et al. 2026; Meta 2020 Election Study package.
counterevidence_boundary: Selected issue attitudes can move; study windows do not rule out cumulative long-run effects.
effect_denominator: Facebook primary attitudinal outcomes allowed roughly ±0.12 SD effects to be ruled out in the like-minded-source experiment; X found precise nulls on partisanship and affective polarization.
cannot_claim: “Long-run platform effects on identity are zero.”
section: F. ALGORITHM OUTCOME AUDIT — DIRECT PAPER ADDITIONS

title: Political-ad removal null
publishable_sentence: Randomized removal of political advertisements from Facebook and Instagram for six weeks before the 2020 U.S. election produced no detectable changes in political knowledge, polarization, perceived election legitimacy, political participation, candidate favourability or turnout.
direct_primary_source: Nature Human Behaviour 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41562-025-02328-w.
counterevidence_boundary: The study does not show every political advertisement is ineffective; small or heterogeneous effects can exist.
effect_denominator: 36,906 Facebook users and 25,925 Instagram users.
cannot_claim: “Political ads never matter.”
chapter_destination: The Limits of Persuasion / Measured Voter.
section: F. ALGORITHM OUTCOME AUDIT — DIRECT PAPER ADDITIONS

title: General-election persuasion is usually small
publishable_sentence: Field experiments generally find that ordinary persuasive campaign contact in competitive U.S. general elections has little average effect on candidate choice.
direct_primary_source: Kalla & Broockman, APSR (2018), *The Minimal Persuasive Effects of Campaign Contact in General Elections*.
counterevidence_boundary: Exceptions can appear where campaigns identify unusually persuadable voters or exploit unusual issue/candidate conditions.
cannot_claim: no campaign contact ever persuades anyone.

title: Professional political-ad benchmark
publishable_sentence: Across 59 randomized tests of real 2016 presidential advertisements, the average immediate effect on vote intention was about 0.7 percentage points and the average effect on candidate favourability was about 0.05 points on a five-point scale.
direct_primary_source: Coppock, Hill & Vavreck, *Science Advances* (2020), DOI 10.1126/sciadv.abc4046.
counterevidence_boundary: One-exposure survey effects are not estimates of an entire campaign.
effect_denominator: 49 ads, 59 experiments, ~34,000 participants.
cannot_claim: cumulative campaign effects equal a single exposure.

title: Campaign experimentation can improve ad selection
publishable_sentence: Campaigns can use randomized experiments to identify advertisements that perform somewhat better than alternatives, even though absolute persuasive effects are generally small.
counterevidence_boundary: Observable ad features did not reliably predict winners across contexts; survey-test effects likely overstate field effects.
effect_denominator: 146 experiments, 617 ads, 51 campaigns, >500,000 respondents; mean immediate vote-choice effects 2.3 pp (2018 downballot), 1.2 pp (2020 downballot), 0.8 pp (2020 presidential).
cannot_claim: experiments reveal a timeless persuasion formula.

title: Digital vote-share field null
publishable_sentence: A high-saturation Facebook/Instagram advertising experiment during the 2018 Florida midterms estimated a Democratic precinct vote-share effect of −0.04 percentage points (SE 0.85).
direct_primary_source: Coppock, Green & Porter, *Research & Politics* (2022), DOI 10.1177/20531680221076901.
counterevidence_boundary: Confidence interval still permits modest positive or negative effects; one campaign/context cannot represent all digital advertising.
effect_denominator: >1.1 million impressions; >100,000 full views.
cannot_claim: all digital advertising has zero electoral effect.

title: Microtargeting customization limit
publishable_sentence: In two preregistered AI persuasion experiments, customized microtargeted messages were not clearly more persuasive than strong generic messages; the designs had power to detect treatment differences on the order of roughly 1.5–2 percentage points.
direct_primary_source: Argyle et al., PNAS (2025), DOI 10.1073/pnas.2412815122.
counterevidence_boundary: Other forms of personalization may perform differently.
effect_denominator: Persuasive treatments moved attitudes roughly 2.5–4 pp versus controls; customization added no clear gain.
cannot_claim: every possible form of personalization is ineffective.

title: Focal-belief targeting
publishable_sentence: Targeting a belief that an individual personally regards as central to an attitude can modestly increase persuasive impact compared with targeting a less-relevant belief.
direct_primary_source: Velez, Liu & Clifford, APSR (2026), DOI 10.1017/S0003055426101622.
counterevidence_boundary: Incremental attitude advantage was small, and real campaigns may not reliably identify focal beliefs at scale.
effect_denominator: pooled incremental effect d=0.054 (SE=0.02); 11/12 comparisons favoured focal targeting.
cannot_claim: campaigns possess a reliable psychological key for each voter.

title: Online News Act purpose
publishable_sentence: Canada’s Online News Act was designed to increase the bargaining power and compensation of Canadian news businesses, not to prohibit news distribution.
direct_primary_source: Canadian Heritage; Justice Canada Charter Statement for Bill C-18.
counterevidence_boundary: Policy design still created incentives that led one major platform to withdraw news.
cannot_claim: Ottawa’s stated objective was to stop Canadians seeing news.

title: Meta warned before enactment
publishable_sentence: Meta publicly warned before Bill C-18 received Royal Assent that it would end news availability on Facebook and Instagram in Canada if the legislation passed in the form it opposed.
direct_primary_source: Meta public statement, May 2023; Royal Assent June 22, 2023.
counterevidence_boundary: Public threat does not establish Parliament’s internal expectation or motive.
cannot_claim: the Meta news withdrawal was unforeseeable.

title: Different intermediary responses to the same law
publishable_sentence: Under the same Canadian news-compensation framework, Google reached a financial agreement while Meta withdrew ordinary news availability, demonstrating that platform strategy mediates regulatory outcomes.
direct_primary_source: Canadian Heritage, CRTC, Meta.
counterevidence_boundary: Platforms differed in business model and legal position.
effect_denominator: Google commitment approximately C$100 million annually, indexed to inflation.
cannot_claim: regulation mechanically determines one platform response.

title: Meta news withdrawal changed the information environment
publishable_sentence: Meta’s news withdrawal sharply reduced engagement with Canadian professional news organizations on Facebook and Instagram while Canadians largely continued using the platforms.
counterevidence_boundary: Some news circulated through screenshots/workarounds; long-run sector effects include Google funding and are not one-dimensional.
effect_denominator: MEO estimated ~85% loss of Meta engagement for Canadian news outlets, ~43% overall social engagement decline, and ~11 million fewer daily Meta news views after one year.
cannot_claim: all Canadians stopped consuming journalism or the Act had only negative sector effects.

title: Author Facebook-ban case
publishable_sentence: The author reports that Facebook permanently disabled his account after he shared a story warning about possible harms associated with peptide-based weight-loss use; the causal basis for the enforcement action is not established from the evidence currently preserved.
direct_primary_source: Author recollection; enforcement records not yet preserved in project.
counterevidence_boundary: Bill C-18 could explain inability to share a recognized news link in Canada after the news block, but not by itself a permanent account disablement. Meta separately uses automated and human Community Standards enforcement.
cannot_claim: government ordered the ban; Bill C-18 caused permanent disablement; Meta intentionally suppressed medically correct information.
chapter_destination: Narrative case — The Gatekeeper You Cannot Question.

title: WEF agenda-shaping mission
publishable_sentence: The World Economic Forum openly describes its role as engaging political, business, academic and civil-society leaders to shape global, regional and industry agendas.
direct_primary_source: WEF Institutional Framework.
counterevidence_boundary: Agenda-setting influence is not legal sovereignty.
cannot_claim: WEF can enact Canadian law.

title: Authentic Schwab cabinet quote
publishable_sentence: At a public Harvard Kennedy School forum in September 2017, Klaus Schwab said the WEF had “penetrate[d] the cabinets” and claimed that at least half of Justin Trudeau’s cabinet consisted of Young Global Leaders.
direct_primary_source: Harvard Kennedy School / Harvard Institute of Politics event record and preserved video.
counterevidence_boundary: A boast is not independent proof of its numerical content.
cannot_claim: the statement itself proves control or the cabinet count.

title: 2017 cabinet-count correction
publishable_sentence: WEF primary records verify several Trudeau cabinet ministers as YGL/YGL alumni by September 2017, but do not support Schwab’s claim that half or more of the roughly thirty-member cabinet held that status.
direct_primary_source: WEF programmes/class announcements for Freeland, Brison, Joly and Champagne; Government of Canada ministry records.
counterevidence_boundary: Additional WEF relationships may exist under categories other than YGL.
cannot_claim: exhaustive absence of all other WEF ties.

title: Cross-party YGL participation
publishable_sentence: Canadian participation in the WEF Young Global Leaders network crossed party lines, including Liberal, Conservative and NDP politicians.
direct_primary_source: WEF 2016 class (Michelle Rempel Garner); WEF 2018 class (Jagmeet Singh); Liberal examples above.
counterevidence_boundary: Cross-party participation does not imply common policy obedience.
cannot_claim: YGL members form a coordinated Canadian political bloc.

title: Poilievre WEF archive / YGL claim
publishable_sentence: An archived April 2021 World Economic Forum `/people/` page for Pierre Poilievre is real and was later removed, but the recovered page does not identify him as a Young Global Leader, and no verified WEF YGL class roster naming him was found in the archive-level search.
counterevidence_boundary: WEF `/people/` pages are broader than YGL membership; current WEF profiles exist for politicians whose profiles do not identify them as YGLs. Page existence therefore proves WEF hosted a profile, not membership or programme participation.
cannot_claim: “Poilievre was never on the WEF website”; “the archived page was fake”; “the deleted profile proves he was a YGL”; “WEF scrubbed a YGL record to conceal membership”; or “Poilievre's explanation has been independently verified by WEF.”
chapter_destination: The WEF Clip Was Real. The Math Wasn't. / Digital Archaeology.

title: Trudeau formal YGL cohort status
publishable_sentence: Justin Trudeau's public relationship with the WEF is well documented, and multiple later compiled sources identify him with the 2005 Young Global Leaders class, but this audit has not yet recovered an original WEF 2005 cohort roster or archived individual profile that closes the formal membership question.
counterevidence_boundary: WEF's 2016 Annual Meeting programme explicitly labels Scott Brison and Chrystia Freeland as YGL/YGL alumnus while listing Trudeau simply as Prime Minister; independent archive researchers disagree on whether his formal YGL status is confirmed.
cannot_claim: “Trudeau is definitively a 2005 YGL” until original WEF cohort evidence is recovered; equally, absence of that recovered document does not erase his extensive documented WEF relationship.
chapter_destination: The WEF Clip Was Real. The Math Wasn't.

title: Carney WEF trustee
publishable_sentence: Mark Carney served for multiple years on the World Economic Forum’s Board of Trustees before becoming Prime Minister of Canada.
direct_primary_source: WEF Board of Trustees records, 2018–2022.
counterevidence_boundary: Trustee status establishes institutional proximity and governance participation, not obedience in later public office.
cannot_claim: Carney takes orders from WEF.

title: Freeland WEF relationship
publishable_sentence: Chrystia Freeland was a WEF Young Global Leader alumnus and later served on the WEF Board of Trustees while holding senior Canadian cabinet office.
direct_primary_source: WEF annual-meeting programmes and governance reports.
counterevidence_boundary: Dual institutional connection creates a transparency question but does not itself prove conflict or capture.
cannot_claim: WEF dictated Freeland’s policies.

title: Canada/WEF digital-identity collaboration
publishable_sentence: Canada publicly collaborated with the WEF and private partners on the Known Traveller Digital Identity prototype using biometrics, cryptography and distributed-ledger technology.
direct_primary_source: Transport Canada, January 25, 2018; WEF project release.
counterevidence_boundary: The project was publicly announced and described as voluntary/user-centric.
cannot_claim: WEF secretly imposed digital identity on Canada.

title: Agile Nations WEF role
publishable_sentence: Canada’s 2020 Agile Nations Charter granted the WEF observer status in a voluntary, non-binding regulatory-cooperation network, including the ability to attend plenaries and make proposals for the work programme.
direct_primary_source: Government of Canada Agile Nations Charter.
counterevidence_boundary: Observer/proposal rights are not legislative authority.
cannot_claim: WEF could write binding Canadian regulations.

title: 2022 Hansard correction
publishable_sentence: The official 2022 House of Commons transcript attributes the interruption of Colin Carrie’s WEF question to poor audio/video; another MP then called the premise disinformation and was himself stopped because the exchange was becoming debate.
direct_primary_source: House of Commons Hansard No. 034, February 19, 2022.
counterevidence_boundary: The exchange still demonstrates political hostility around the subject.
cannot_claim: the transcript proves Carrie was censored simply for mentioning WEF.

title: Government-deception epistemic rule
publishable_sentence: Documented government cover stories justify greater skepticism and independent verification, but they do not reverse the burden of proof for unrelated claims.
counterevidence_boundary: Some secrecy is lawful and some official statements are accurate.
cannot_claim: because a government lied before, its current denial proves the opposite.

title: UAP versus extraterrestrial evidence
publishable_sentence: U.S. authorities acknowledge and investigate unresolved UAP reports, but current official reviews report no verifiable evidence that UAP represent extraterrestrial beings or technology.
direct_primary_source: Department of Defense / AARO historical and annual reports.
counterevidence_boundary: Some cases remain unresolved because available data are inadequate.
cannot_claim: “unidentified” means “alien,” or that official review has confirmed extraterrestrial craft.
chapter_destination: Past Lies, Present Burden of Proof.

title: Borden government deliberately altered electorate composition
publishable_sentence: Facing a 1917 election dominated by conscription, Robert Borden's government deliberately changed the federal electorate in ways expected to strengthen the government's electoral position.
counterevidence_boundary: Wartime voting presented genuine administrative and democratic problems, including enfranchising large numbers of servicemembers overseas.
cannot_claim: every provision had only a partisan purpose, or the government fabricated the underlying wartime problem.

title: Selective women's enfranchisement
publishable_sentence: The War-time Elections Act extended the federal vote to selected close female relatives of servicemembers in categories the government expected to be more favourable to conscription, while some provincially enfranchised women without the qualifying military relationship could lose the federal vote.
effect_denominator: Elections Canada estimates roughly 500,000 names were added to electoral lists through the wartime female-relative franchise.
cannot_claim: every newly enfranchised woman supported Borden, or women had to promise to vote Conservative.

title: Wartime disenfranchisement
publishable_sentence: The War-time Elections Act disenfranchised categories including certain naturalized British subjects associated with enemy countries and conscientious objectors, with tens of thousands of new Canadians on the Prairies affected.
counterevidence_boundary: Exact individual political preferences cannot be inferred from the legal categories.
cannot_claim: every disenfranchised citizen opposed conscription or would have voted Laurier Liberal.

title: Military-vote allocation changed seats
publishable_sentence: More than 90% of the 1917 military vote supported the government side, and Elections Canada reports that redistribution of military votes changed at least fourteen constituency outcomes in the Conservatives' favour.
effect_denominator: At least 14 seats; final House result 153 Government/Unionist to 82 Laurier Liberal.
cannot_claim: those fourteen seats alone determined who formed government.

title: “Stolen election” counterfactual
publishable_sentence: The 1917 election was conducted under rules deliberately engineered for partisan advantage, but the surviving evidence does not establish that Borden would have lost under a neutral-rule counterfactual.
counterevidence_boundary: Selective enfranchisement, disenfranchisement, government-appointed enumerators, irregularities and campaign effects may have altered additional outcomes.
cannot_claim: “Borden mathematically stole the election” or “Laurier definitely wins without the 1917 laws.”
chapter_destination: Who Counted as “The People”? / Myths We Killed.

title: House as direct popular branch, with state-defined electorate
publishable_sentence: The Constitution made the House the federal branch most directly connected to voters, requiring representatives to be chosen every two years by the people while tying voter qualifications to those used for the most numerous branch of each state legislature.
direct_primary_source: U.S. Constitution, Article I, §2, cl.1; Constitution Annotated.
counterevidence_boundary: The Constitution did not create a universal federal electorate.
cannot_claim: universal popular federal suffrage was established in 1787.
section: J. U.S. FOUNDING ARCHITECTURE PRIMARY-SOURCE CLOSEOUT

title: Original Senate filtration
publishable_sentence: The original Senate deliberately placed greater institutional distance between ordinary voters and federal lawmaking through state-legislative selection, six-year terms, and staggered turnover.
direct_primary_source: U.S. Constitution, Article I, §3; Federalist Nos. 62–63.
counterevidence_boundary: Senate design also served state equality, federal compromise, institutional stability and state sovereignty; anti-popular cooling was not the sole purpose.
cannot_claim: the Senate existed only to suppress popular rule.
section: J. U.S. FOUNDING ARCHITECTURE PRIMARY-SOURCE CLOSEOUT

title: Presidential direct popular vote not constitutionally required
publishable_sentence: Article II did not require direct popular election of the President; states were to appoint electors in whatever manner their legislatures directed.
direct_primary_source: U.S. Constitution, Article II, §1, cl.2; Convention history in Constitution Annotated.
counterevidence_boundary: States later moved toward popular election of electors.
cannot_claim: the original Constitution required a national popular presidential vote.
section: J. U.S. FOUNDING ARCHITECTURE PRIMARY-SOURCE CLOSEOUT

title: Judicial insulation
publishable_sentence: Article III insulated federal judges from ordinary electoral turnover by granting tenure during good behaviour and protecting compensation.
direct_primary_source: U.S. Constitution, Article III, §1.
counterevidence_boundary: Judges are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate; independence is not complete political isolation.
cannot_claim: federal judges were designed to be directly democratically accountable through elections.
section: J. U.S. FOUNDING ARCHITECTURE PRIMARY-SOURCE CLOSEOUT

title: Amendment supermajoritarianism
publishable_sentence: Article V deliberately requires consent beyond an ordinary national majority, using two-thirds thresholds for proposal and ratification by three-fourths of states.
direct_primary_source: U.S. Constitution, Article V.
cannot_claim: a national 50%+1 vote can amend the Constitution.
section: J. U.S. FOUNDING ARCHITECTURE PRIMARY-SOURCE CLOSEOUT

title: Madison popular foundation plus filtration
publishable_sentence: Madison argued at the Convention that direct popular election of one legislative branch was essential to free government while also defending “successive filtrations” for more remote offices.
direct_primary_source: Madison's Convention notes, May 31, 1787.
counterevidence_boundary: Madison warned filtration could be pushed too far.
cannot_claim: Madison wanted either direct popular control over every office or removal of the people from the constitutional foundation.
section: J. U.S. FOUNDING ARCHITECTURE PRIMARY-SOURCE CLOSEOUT

title: Extended sphere against faction
publishable_sentence: Madison explicitly argued that enlarging the republic and multiplying interests could make it harder for a majority faction to coordinate oppression.
direct_primary_source: Federalist No. 10; Hamilton's Convention notes recording Madison's “enlarge the sphere” argument.
counterevidence_boundary: Brutus argued the opposite prediction: scale would destroy meaningful representation and accountability.
cannot_claim: the extended-republic theory was uncontested or empirically guaranteed.
section: J. U.S. FOUNDING ARCHITECTURE PRIMARY-SOURCE CLOSEOUT

title: Hamilton executive energy plus accountability
publishable_sentence: Hamilton defended an energetic executive as necessary for effective government while pairing executive energy with republican dependence on the people and responsibility.
direct_primary_source: Federalist No. 70.
cannot_claim: Hamilton simply advocated unconstrained executive power.
section: J. U.S. FOUNDING ARCHITECTURE PRIMARY-SOURCE CLOSEOUT

title: Adams representation plus checks
publishable_sentence: John Adams argued that large societies require representative government and that the representative assembly should reflect the people, while warning that a single unchecked assembly could succumb to passion, prejudice and hasty judgment.
direct_primary_source: John Adams, *Thoughts on Government* (1776).
cannot_claim: Adams simply rejected democracy or popular representation.
section: J. U.S. FOUNDING ARCHITECTURE PRIMARY-SOURCE CLOSEOUT

title: Anti-Federalist scale/distance critique
publishable_sentence: Brutus accepted the need for representation but argued that a republic as large as the proposed United States would leave representatives too distant and officials too difficult for ordinary people to control.
direct_primary_source: Brutus I, October 18, 1787.
counterevidence_boundary: Federalist No. 10 treated the same geographic scale as a protection against majority faction.
cannot_claim: Anti-Federalists simply opposed representative government.
section: J. U.S. FOUNDING ARCHITECTURE PRIMARY-SOURCE CLOSEOUT

title: No single Founders' intent
publishable_sentence: The constitutional settlement emerged from substantial disagreement among delegates and ratifiers over popular election, institutional distance, state power, representation, executive strength and the proper scale of republican government.
cannot_claim: “the Founders wanted X” as a precise psychological claim without specifying the actor, institution or genuinely shared principle.
section: J. U.S. FOUNDING ARCHITECTURE PRIMARY-SOURCE CLOSEOUT

title: System-level popular legitimacy + mediation synthesis
publishable_sentence: The Constitution placed popular authority at the foundation of federal government while deliberately mediating ordinary popular control through representation, state institutions, indirect selection, staggered tenure, judicial independence, divided authority and difficult constitutional change.
counterevidence_boundary: Different institutions had different purposes; the House was deliberately direct; filtering is not a sufficient single-cause explanation of the Constitution.
cannot_claim: the whole Constitution was designed solely to protect elites from voters.
section: J. U.S. FOUNDING ARCHITECTURE PRIMARY-SOURCE CLOSEOUT

title: Actual smartphone use and delay discounting
publishable_sentence: In observational research using actual phone-use data, heavier smartphone use is associated with steeper delay discounting and lower self-control, with similar relationships for social-media and gaming use.
direct_primary_source: Schulz van Endert & Mohr, *PLOS ONE* (2020), DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0241383.
counterevidence_boundary: Observational design cannot determine whether heavy use causes impatience or people high in delay discounting use smartphones more heavily.
effect_denominator: n=101; net screen time vs larger-delayed-reward choices r≈−0.25; net screen time vs log discount parameter r≈0.21; self-control r≈−0.32.
cannot_claim: smartphones caused a population-wide loss of delayed gratification.
section: K. VANISHING PAUSE / SMARTPHONE ATTENTION CLOSEOUT

title: Delay-discounting causality unresolved
publishable_sentence: Existing experimental evidence does not cleanly establish that smartphone exposure itself causes a durable increase in delay discounting.
cannot_claim: phones trained a generation to prefer immediate rewards.
chapter_destination: The Vanishing Pause / Myths We Killed.
section: K. VANISHING PAUSE / SMARTPHONE ATTENTION CLOSEOUT

title: Notification scheduling changes interruption experience
publishable_sentence: A randomized two-week field experiment found that batching smartphone notifications three times daily reduced reported interruption and stress and improved reported attention, productivity, mood and control, whereas eliminating notifications entirely increased anxiety and fear of missing out.
direct_primary_source: Fitz et al., *Computers in Human Behavior* 101 (2019), DOI 10.1016/j.chb.2019.07.016.
counterevidence_boundary: Many outcomes were self-reported; hourly batching produced little change.
cannot_claim: turning off every notification necessarily improves attention or well-being.
section: K. VANISHING PAUSE / SMARTPHONE ATTENTION CLOSEOUT

title: Blocking mobile internet can improve sustained attention
publishable_sentence: A preregistered randomized trial found that blocking mobile-internet access on smartphones for two weeks produced a modest improvement in objectively measured sustained attention.
direct_primary_source: Castelo et al., *PNAS Nexus* (2025), DOI 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgaf017.
counterevidence_boundary: Compliance was difficult: 266 set up the block and 119 met strict preregistered compliance; the intervention blocked all mobile internet rather than identifying a single app/mechanism.
effect_denominator: 467 initially agreed; pooled ITT pre/post sustained-attention effect d_z≈0.23; delayed-treatment replication d_z≈0.28.
cannot_claim: smartphones cause permanent cognitive damage, or social media specifically caused the effect.
section: K. VANISHING PAUSE / SMARTPHONE ATTENTION CLOSEOUT

title: Disordered screen use and cognition
publishable_sentence: Cross-sectional meta-analysis finds that people classified with disordered screen-use behaviours perform worse on average on attention and executive-function measures.
direct_primary_source: Moshel et al., *Neuropsychology Review* 34 (2024), DOI 10.1007/s11065-023-09612-4.
counterevidence_boundary: Cross-sectional; samples skew young/Asian/male; “disordered” use is not ordinary smartphone ownership.
effect_denominator: 34 meta-analysed studies; 1,076 disordered-use participants + 1,338 controls; overall g≈0.38; attention g≈0.50; executive function g≈0.31; high heterogeneity.
cannot_claim: normal smartphone use causes the same deficits.
section: K. VANISHING PAUSE / SMARTPHONE ATTENTION CLOSEOUT

title: Mere-presence “brain drain” is limited
publishable_sentence: A meta-analysis of 56 studies found only limited evidence that the mere presence of a smartphone broadly impairs cognition, with a significant pooled effect for working memory but null pooled effects for the other examined cognitive domains.
counterevidence_boundary: Methodological heterogeneity and generally low statistical power limit certainty.
cannot_claim: a nearby phone universally drains cognitive ability.
chapter_destination: The Vanishing Pause / Myths We Killed.
section: K. VANISHING PAUSE / SMARTPHONE ATTENTION CLOSEOUT

title: The Vanishing Pause hypothesis
publishable_sentence: Smartphones have reduced access, interruption, stopping and response friction; some experiments show that restoring portions of that friction can improve attention-related outcomes, but the downstream effect on political judgment and critical thinking remains unestablished.
counterevidence_boundary: no direct experiment currently demonstrates that added smartphone friction improves political reasoning or reduces polarization.
cannot_claim: the Vanishing Pause is a proven causal mechanism of democratic decline.
chapter_destination: The Vanishing Pause / Why Am I in a Hurry?
section: K. VANISHING PAUSE / SMARTPHONE ATTENTION CLOSEOUT

title: National Register versus party list
publishable_sentence: Elections Canada maintains gender and date of birth in the National Register of Electors, but the annual elector lists distributed to federal political parties contain names, civic and mailing addresses, and the elector's unique identifier rather than the full Register record.
direct_primary_source: Canada Elections Act, ss.44–45; Elections Canada annual-list guidance.
cannot_claim: parties receive the full National Register or receive gender/date of birth on the annual party list.
section: L. CANADIAN POLITICAL DATA / PRIVACY 2026 CLOSEOUT

title: Authorized use of official elector lists
publishable_sentence: Registered parties may use official elector lists to communicate with electors, including soliciting contributions and recruiting members, and the Canada Elections Act prohibits knowingly using list information for unauthorized purposes.
direct_primary_source: Canada Elections Act, ss.110–111; Elections Canada Guidelines for Use of Lists of Electors.
cannot_claim: official list information may lawfully be used for any purpose once received.
section: L. CANADIAN POLITICAL DATA / PRIVACY 2026 CLOSEOUT

title: Richer party databases
publishable_sentence: Federal parties can build political databases containing substantially more information than the official elector list through memberships, donations, petitions, web forms, events, voter contact, public sources and other information they lawfully collect.
counterevidence_boundary: A policy describing possible collection does not prove every field exists for every person or identify the source of every field.
cannot_claim: Elections Canada supplied those richer fields.
section: L. CANADIAN POLITICAL DATA / PRIVACY 2026 CLOSEOUT

title: Commercial-data claim remains party-specific
publishable_sentence: Current public evidence supports richer party profiling from political interaction, public sources and online activity, but any claim that a particular federal party currently purchases broad commercial consumer datasets requires a current party-specific receipt.
counterevidence_boundary: Historic campaign/data literature documents commercial segmentation, but it should not be silently converted into a 2026 universal practice.
cannot_claim: every major federal party buys “all your consumer data.”
chapter_destination: The Measured Canadian / Myths We Killed.
section: L. CANADIAN POLITICAL DATA / PRIVACY 2026 CLOSEOUT

title: Special national Elections Act privacy regime
publishable_sentence: The Canada Elections Act expressly creates a national, uniform, exclusive and complete regime governing registered and eligible federal parties' political activities involving personal information and generally displaces provincial/territorial privacy rules for those activities.
direct_primary_source: Canada Elections Act, ss.446.2–446.4.
counterevidence_boundary: Other applicable federal laws still apply; a party policy may provide otherwise for provincial-law application.
cannot_claim: parties operate outside all privacy law.
section: L. CANADIAN POLITICAL DATA / PRIVACY 2026 CLOSEOUT

title: Privacy Act/PIPEDA distinction
publishable_sentence: Federal political parties are not subject to the federal Privacy Act or PIPEDA as their general political-party data regime; their principal privacy obligations are instead contained in the Canada Elections Act.
direct_primary_source: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, May 2026 Bill C-25 submissions.
cannot_claim: federal parties have no privacy obligations.
section: L. CANADIAN POLITICAL DATA / PRIVACY 2026 CLOSEOUT

title: Bill C-76 lineage
publishable_sentence: Parliament first required federal political parties to develop, submit and publish privacy policies through the 2018 Elections Modernization Act (Bill C-76).
direct_primary_source: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada; legislative history.
cannot_claim: Bill C-47 or Bill C-25 created the original party privacy-policy requirement.
section: L. CANADIAN POLITICAL DATA / PRIVACY 2026 CLOSEOUT

title: Bill C-25 safeguards
publishable_sentence: Bill C-25, which received Royal Assent on June 18, 2026, adds requirements for proportionate security safeguards, breach response and qualifying individual notification, equivalent protection for transferred data, and prohibitions on misleading collection explanations, sale of personal information and public disclosure intended to cause harm.
direct_primary_source: Bill C-25 third-reading/enacted provisions; Elections Canada July 2026 implementation guidance.
cannot_claim: every party's August 2026 website policy already contains the post-September requirements.
section: L. CANADIAN POLITICAL DATA / PRIVACY 2026 CLOSEOUT

title: Remaining privacy gaps
publishable_sentence: The Privacy Commissioner welcomed Bill C-25's improvements while recommending statutory baseline requirements for consent, purpose/collection/use limitation, access and correction, breach reporting to an independent regulator and stronger independent oversight.
direct_primary_source: OPC May 14 and May 28, 2026 submissions.
counterevidence_boundary: Parties may voluntarily provide stronger rights in their own policies; the recommendation is not itself law.
cannot_claim: Bill C-25 gives electors a full PIPEDA-style right to inspect/correct political profiles.
section: L. CANADIAN POLITICAL DATA / PRIVACY 2026 CLOSEOUT

title: Privacy survives weak persuasion
publishable_sentence: A privacy concern can exist even when targeted persuasion has little effect, because invisible classification, inferred preferences and asymmetric access to personal profiles affect autonomy independently of message effectiveness.
cannot_claim: privacy harm automatically proves manipulation or electoral effect.
chapter_destination: You Don't Get to Know Me Well Enough to Optimize Me.
